title: The French Revolution
brief: In ten stormy years, France went from an absolute king to a radical republic and then to Napoleon. Let's trace the pressures that drove each dramatic turn.

questions.question: What mix of money and food crises pushed France toward revolution in 1789?
questions.answer: Costly foreign wars left the crown nearly bankrupt while nobles and clergy paid almost no taxes. Bad harvests then sent bread prices soaring, so ordinary families could barely feed themselves.
key_points: War debt pushed the crown near bankruptcy, or unfair rules let nobles and clergy skip taxes
Poor harvests made bread prices skyrocket and left ordinary people hungry
Commoners carried almost the entire tax burden while struggling to buy daily food
questions.hint: Think of an empty royal treasury, a lopsided bill dumped on workers, and growling stomachs after harsh winters.
questions.fun_fact: Paying for the American Revolution helped bankrupt King Louis the Sixteenth, and by early 1789 a single loaf of bread ate up most of a Parisian worker's daily pay.

questions.question: Why did Parisians storm a nearly empty Bastille, and why did its fall shake all of France?
questions.answer: The crowd attacked the fortress to grab stored gunpowder for weapons against nearby royal troops. The Bastille symbolized unchecked royal power, so its fall sparked wider revolt across France. For the first time, ordinary street crowds showed they could overpower the crown.
key_points: Parisians stormed it to seize gunpowder for their weapons
It symbolized unchecked royal power, or its fall sparked popular revolt across France
Only seven prisoners were inside, none of them major political heroes
questions.hint: Picture citizens carrying unloaded rifles who also want to tear down the monarchy's most famous stone threat.
questions.fun_fact: After the fortress came down, the Marquis de Lafayette mailed its main iron key to George Washington, and it still hangs at Mount Vernon today.

questions.question: How did a fight over voting rules at the Estates-General spark the Tennis Court Oath?
questions.answer: Each estate got one collective vote, so nobles and clergy could always outvote commoners two to one. The Third Estate demanded individual votes, broke away, and declared itself the National Assembly. When guards locked their hall, deputies gathered in a tennis court and swore to write a constitution.
key_points: Voting by estate let nobles and clergy outvote commoners two to one, while the Third Estate demanded one vote per person
That deadlock pushed commoners to break away and vow to stay together until they wrote a constitution
When royal guards locked their usual hall, deputies met in an indoor tennis court instead
questions.hint: Think about 98 percent of the country getting overruled by tiny privileged groups, and lawmakers refusing to go home.
questions.fun_fact: Out of 577 deputies in that court, just one man refused to sign, insisting he could not act without royal approval.

questions.concept: Rights of Man and its limits
questions.question: What big political idea did the Declaration of the Rights of Man introduce, and who did it still leave out?
questions.answer: It declared that sovereign power belongs to the nation, not the king. It also promised citizens equal rights under law, ending noble birth privileges. Yet it excluded women from full citizenship and left slavery intact across France's colonies.
key_points: Sovereignty belongs to the nation rather than the king, or citizens are born free and equal under the law
It still left out women or enslaved people in French colonies
It protected basic freedoms like speech, property, and resisting oppression
questions.hint: Ask where authority moves when a crown loses its divine claim, and notice both the narrow title and overseas sugar islands.
questions.fun_fact: Playwright Olympe de Gouges fired back in 1791 with her own Rights of Woman, arguing that if women could be sent to the scaffold, they deserved to speak in parliament.

questions.question: How did King Louis the Sixteenth's failed escape at Varennes wreck the plan for a constitutional monarchy?
questions.answer: Sneaking out of Paris in disguise proved the king hated the revolution and never truly accepted sharing power. He tried to reach loyal troops near the border, which looked like treason to furious citizens. Public trust collapsed overnight, turning many French people away from keeping any king at all.
key_points: Fleeing in disguise shattered public trust by proving the king opposed the revolution, or made him look like a traitor
A constitutional monarchy only worked if people believed the king would cooperate with elected lawmakers
The backlash boosted radical calls to abolish the throne and create a republic
questions.hint: Imagine signing a peace deal with a partner, then catching them climbing out the back window at midnight.
questions.fun_fact: A sharp-eyed village postmaster named Jean-Baptiste Drouet spotted the disguised king during a carriage stop and rode ahead to halt the royal family at Varennes.

questions.question: Why did France go to war in 1792, and how did battlefield crisis push the Montagnards past the Girondins?
questions.answer: Girondin leaders pushed for war against Austria to rally the nation and expose royal treason. Early defeats, internal revolts, and scarce food then sparked fierce anger among working-class Parisian sans-culottes. Montagnards backed harsh emergency measures to win street support, while hesitant Girondins were purged from power.
key_points: Girondins wanted war to unite France, spread revolutionary ideals, or expose the king's disloyalty
War defeats and revolts drove Montagnards to back harsh emergency rules and ally with angry Paris workers, overtaking moderate Girondins
Armed Parisian sans-culottes surrounded the assembly in 1793 and forced the arrest of Girondin leaders
questions.hint: Think about gambling on foreign combat to steady a shaky government, only to watch panic reward the toughest faction.
questions.fun_fact: Paris's militant workers took the name sans-culottes, meaning without knee breeches, because wearing long trousers marked them against silk-clad aristocrats.

questions.question: How did Robespierre justify the Reign of Terror, and why did his own colleagues finally turn against him?
questions.answer: Robespierre argued that civic virtue alone was helpless in a crisis without swift terror to crush enemies. The Committee of Public Safety used that logic to arrest suspects and guillotine thousands across France. Lawmakers finally overthrew him in the Thermidorian Reaction because everyone feared his next list of traitors.
key_points: He claimed republican virtue needed terror behind it to defend the revolution and crush internal or foreign enemies
Fellow lawmakers overthrew him out of self-preservation because they feared being accused and executed next
His fall in July 1794 launched the Thermidorian Reaction, which dismantled the Terror and closed the Jacobin Club
questions.hint: Think about guarding pure ideals with harsh force, and what happens to a room of politicians when nobody feels secure.
questions.fun_fact: Despite its reputation for hunting nobles, the vast majority of the roughly 17,000 people officially executed during the Terror were ordinary commoners.

questions.question: Why did the Directory fail to stabilize France, and what revolutionary bargain did Napoleon strike after seizing power?
questions.answer: The Directory faced raging inflation, rampant corruption, and constant attacks from both royalists and radical Jacobins. It survived only by canceling elections and leaning on the army, which invited Napoleon's coup in 1799. Napoleon kept major revolutionary gains like legal equality and property rights, while ending political freedom.
key_points: The Directory suffered from corruption, runaway inflation, or constant clashes with royalists and radicals, forcing it to rely on the army
Napoleon preserved revolutionary gains like legal equality and property rights while taking away political freedom
His takeover in the coup of 18 Brumaire replaced the Directory with the Consulate
questions.hint: Picture a battered middle hated by opposing extremes, then ask what exhausted citizens gave up to get order.
questions.fun_fact: Because France's revolutionary calendar named its misty autumn month Brumaire, meaning fog, Napoleon's takeover is literally remembered as the Coup of 18 Fog.

tagline: From bread riots to Napoleon in ten years
